name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q24 - Strongest Bronsted base among given amines

questiontext.text: 24. Among the following amines, the strongest Brönsted base is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A Brönsted base is a proton acceptor, and its basic strength depends on the availability of the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom for protonation. Localized lone pairs on \(sp^3\)-hybridized nitrogen atoms with electron-donating alkyl groups are more available than delocalized lone pairs.

Step 2: Evaluation
In aniline, the lone pair on the nitrogen atom is delocalized into the benzene ring through resonance, reducing its availability for protonation. In pyrrole, the lone pair on the nitrogen atom participates in the aromatic sextet (\(6\pi\) electrons), making it unavailable for protonation without destroying aromaticity. Ammonia (\(\mathrm{NH}_3\)) has a localized lone pair on \(sp^3\)-hybridized nitrogen, but lacks electron-donating alkyl groups.

Step 3: Application
In pyrrolidine (the saturated five-membered cyclic secondary amine), the nitrogen atom is \(sp^3\)-hybridized, its lone pair is completely localized, and it is bonded to two electron-donating alkyl carbons (\(+I\) effect), which increases electron density on nitrogen and stabilizes the conjugate acid.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, pyrrolidine is the strongest Brönsted base among the given compounds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q25 - Decreasing order of basic strength of species

questiontext.text:
25. The correct decreasing order of basic strength of the following species is

\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}, \mathrm{NH}_3, \mathrm{OH}^-, \mathrm{NH}_2^-\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Basic strength increases with the availability of an electron pair for protonation. Negatively charged species are stronger bases than their neutral conjugate acids, and a less electronegative atom holds its lone pair less tightly, making it a stronger base.

Step 2: Evaluation
Comparing the negatively charged anions \(\mathrm{NH}_2^-\) and \(\mathrm{OH}^-\), nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so \(\mathrm{NH}_2^-\) donates its lone pair more readily than \(\mathrm{OH}^-\). Similarly, comparing the neutral molecules \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, making \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) a stronger base than \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

Step 3: Application
Since anions are stronger bases than neutral molecules (\(\mathrm{OH}^-\) is the conjugate base of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) and is much stronger than \(\mathrm{NH}_3\)), the overall decreasing order of basic strength is \(\mathrm{NH}_2^- > \mathrm{OH}^- > \mathrm{NH}_3 > \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct decreasing order of basic strength is \(\mathrm{NH}_2^- > \mathrm{OH}^- > \mathrm{NH}_3 > \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q26 - Most volatile compound among amines and alkane

questiontext.text:
26. Which of the following should be most volatile?

(I) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{NH}_2\)    (II) \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{N}\)    (III) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{NHCH}_3\)    (IV) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Volatility is inversely related to boiling point, which depends on the strength of intermolecular forces and molecular mass. Compounds with weaker intermolecular forces have lower boiling points and higher volatility.

Step 2: Evaluation
Propan-1-amine (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{NH}_2\)) and N-methylethanamine (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{NHCH}_3\)) possess \(\mathrm{N-H}\) bonds and exhibit strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Trimethylamine (\((\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{N}\)) lacks \(\mathrm{N-H}\) bonds, so it has no intermolecular hydrogen bonding, but still experiences polar dipole–dipole interactions due to its polar \(\mathrm{C-N}\) bonds.

Step 3: Application
Propane (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\)) is a nonpolar hydrocarbon with only weak London dispersion forces and also has the lowest molar mass (\(44\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) compared to the isomeric amines (\(59\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)). Consequently, propane has the lowest boiling point.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, propane (IV) is the most volatile compound among the given species.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q27 - Preparation of amines retaining carbon chain length

questiontext.text: 27. Which of the following methods of preparation of amines will give same number of carbon atoms in the chain of amines as in the reactant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis, an alkyl halide (\(\mathrm{R-X}\)) reacts with potassium phthalimide followed by hydrolysis to yield a primary amine (\(\mathrm{R-NH}_2\)) without adding or removing any carbon atoms from the alkyl chain \(\mathrm{R}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
In contrast, Hofmann bromamide degradation (treatment of an amide \(\mathrm{R-CONH}_2\) with \(\mathrm{Br}_2\) in aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\)) yields an amine (\(\mathrm{R-NH}_2\)) containing one carbon atom less than the parent amide. Reduction of an amide (\(\mathrm{R-CONH}_2\)) with \(\mathrm{LiAlH}_4\) converts the carbonyl carbon into a \(-\mathrm{CH}_2-\) group, and nitrites (\(\mathrm{R-ONO}\)) are esters of nitrous acid rather than standard precursors to primary amines of the same chain.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Heating an alkyl halide with the potassium salt of phthalimide followed by hydrolysis gives a primary amine with the same number of carbon atoms in the chain as in the reactant alkyl halide.

answer.text: Reaction of amide with \(\mathrm{LiAlH}_4\) followed by treatment with water.
Heating alkylhalide with potassium salt of phthalimide followed by hydrolysis.
Treatment of amide with bromine in aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q28 - Haloarenes not prepared by Sandmeyer reaction

questiontext.text: 28. Which of the following cannot be prepared by Sandmeyer's reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sandmeyer's reaction involves treating an aryldiazonium salt with copper(I) halides (\(\mathrm{CuCl/HCl}\) or \(\mathrm{CuBr/HBr}\)) or \(\mathrm{CuCN/KCN}\) to introduce \(-\mathrm{Cl}\), \(-\mathrm{Br}\), or \(-\mathrm{CN}\) onto the aromatic ring.

Step 2: Evaluation
Chlorobenzene and bromobenzene are readily prepared by Sandmeyer's reaction using \(\mathrm{CuCl/HCl}\) and \(\mathrm{CuBr/HBr}\), respectively. However, iodobenzene is prepared by warming the diazonium salt with aqueous \(\mathrm{KI}\) (without a copper(I) catalyst), and fluorobenzene is prepared by the Balz–Schiemann reaction (treating the diazonium salt with \(\mathrm{HBF}_4\) followed by thermal decomposition of the fluoroborate salt).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, iodobenzene and fluorobenzene cannot be prepared by Sandmeyer's reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q29 - Reagents reducing nitrobenzene to aniline

questiontext.text: 29. Reduction of nitrobenzene by which of the following reagent gives aniline?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aromatic nitro compounds such as nitrobenzene are reduced to primary aromatic amines (aniline) either by catalytic hydrogenation or by active metals in acidic medium.

Step 2: Evaluation
Using \(\mathrm{Sn/HCl}\), \(\mathrm{Fe/HCl}\), or \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{-Pd}\) efficiently reduces the \(-\mathrm{NO}_2\) group of nitrobenzene to \(-\mathrm{NH}_2\), yielding aniline. In contrast, \(\mathrm{Sn/NH}_4\mathrm{OH}\) does not provide the acidic medium required for complete reduction of nitrobenzene to aniline.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(\mathrm{Sn/HCl}\), \(\mathrm{Fe/HCl}\), and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{-Pd}\) are the reagents that reduce nitrobenzene to aniline.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q30 - Species involved in carbylamine test

questiontext.text: 30. Which of the following species are involved in the carbylamine test?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The carbylamine test (isocyanide test) is a characteristic reaction of primary aliphatic and aromatic amines used to distinguish them from secondary and tertiary amines.

Step 2: Evaluation
When a primary amine (\(\mathrm{R-NH}_2\)) is heated with chloroform (\(\mathrm{CHCl}_3\)) and ethanolic potassium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{KOH}\)), it forms a foul-smelling isocyanide (carbylamine, \(\mathrm{R-NC}\)):

\[\mathrm{R-NH}_2 + \mathrm{CHCl}_3 + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R-NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]

Phosgene (\(\mathrm{COCl}_2\)) and nitrous acid (\(\mathrm{NaNO}_2 + \mathrm{HCl}\)) are not part of the carbylamine reaction.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{R-NC}\) and \(\mathrm{CHCl}_3\) are the species involved in the carbylamine test.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q31 - Reagents converting benzenediazonium chloride to benzene

questiontext.text: 31. The reagents that can be used to convert benzenediazonium chloride to benzene are

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mild reducing agents such as hypophosphorous acid (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\)) in water or ethanol (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH}\)) reduce aryldiazonium salts to the corresponding arenes by replacing the diazonium group with a hydrogen atom.

Step 2: Evaluation
Benzenediazonium chloride reacts with \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) to give benzene, \(\mathrm{N}_2\), \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_3\), and \(\mathrm{HCl}\). Similarly, ethanol reduces benzenediazonium chloride to benzene while being oxidized to ethanal (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO}\)). In contrast, \(\mathrm{SnCl}_2/\mathrm{HCl}\) reduces benzenediazonium chloride to phenylhydrazine, and \(\mathrm{LiAlH}_4\) is not used for this conversion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) can be used to convert benzenediazonium chloride to benzene.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q32 - Product of bromination of acetanilide in acetic acid

questiontext.text: 32. The product of the following reaction is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The acetamido group (\(-\mathrm{NHCOCH}_3\)) on the benzene ring is moderately activating and ortho, para-directing toward electrophilic aromatic substitution. Because the lone pair on nitrogen is partially delocalized into the carbonyl group, its activating power is much lower than that of \(-\mathrm{NH}_2\), preventing polysubstitution.

Step 2: Evaluation
When acetanilide reacts with \(\mathrm{Br}_2\) in ethanoic acid (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}\)), monobromination occurs at the para position (major product, p-bromoacetanilide) and at the ortho position (minor product, o-bromoacetanilide). Meta substitution and 2,4,6-tribromination do not occur under these conditions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, both p-bromoacetanilide and o-bromoacetanilide are formed as products of this reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q33 - Arenium ion involved in bromination of aniline

questiontext.text: 33. Arenium ion involved in the bromination of aniline is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The amino group (\(-\mathrm{NH}_2\)) is a strongly activating, ortho, para-directing group in electrophilic aromatic substitution. Electrophilic attack by \(\mathrm{Br}^+\) therefore occurs at the ortho and para positions relative to \(-\mathrm{NH}_2\), forming resonance-stabilized arenium ions (\(\sigma\)-complexes).

Step 2: Evaluation
Attack at the ortho position places the positive charge at the positions ortho and para to the newly formed \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond—specifically at the carbon bearing \(-\mathrm{NH}_2\) (stabilized by resonance with the nitrogen lone pair to give \(=\mathrm{NH}_2^+\)) and at the other ring carbons in the conjugated system. Similarly, attack at the para position gives a \(\sigma\)-complex stabilized by the \(=\mathrm{NH}_2^+\) iminium resonance contributor. An arenium ion resulting from meta attack (with \(\mathrm{Br}\) at the meta carbon) is not formed because the \(-\mathrm{NH}_2\) group cannot stabilize the positive charge in that intermediate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the ortho-substituted arenium ion resonance structures and the para-substituted arenium ion resonance structure are involved in the bromination of aniline.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q34 - Amines prepared by Gabriel synthesis

questiontext.text: 34. Which of the following amines can be prepared by Gabriel synthesis.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is used exclusively to prepare primary aliphatic amines (including arylalkyl primary amines) via an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction between the phthalimide anion and an unhindered alkyl halide, followed by hydrolysis.

Step 2: Evaluation
Isobutylamine (\((\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\mathrm{CHCH}_2\mathrm{NH}_2\)) and 2-phenylethylamine (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{NH}_2\)) are primary aliphatic amines whose corresponding primary alkyl halides readily undergo \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) substitution with potassium phthalimide. N-Methylbenzylamine is a secondary amine and cannot be formed by this method. Aniline is a primary aromatic amine, and aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion under these conditions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, isobutyl amine and 2-phenylethylamine can be prepared by Gabriel synthesis.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q35 - Identifying correct organic reactions of alkyl halides and amines

questiontext.text: 35. Which of the following reactions are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Primary alkyl halides undergo nucleophilic substitution (ammonolysis) with excess ammonia to form primary amines and ammonium salts. Cycloalkyl halides undergo \(\beta\)-elimination (dehydrohalogenation) when heated with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) to form cycloalkenes.

Step 2: Evaluation
The reaction of ethyl chloride with excess \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) correctly yields ethylamine and \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl}\). Similarly, chlorocyclohexane treated with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) undergoes dehydrohalogenation to give cyclohexene. In contrast, treating tert-butyl chloride with aqueous \(\mathrm{KOH}\) favors nucleophilic substitution to form tert-butyl alcohol rather than elimination, and treating propan-1-amine with \(\mathrm{HNO}_2\) at \(0^\circ\mathrm{C}\) yields a three-carbon alcohol rather than a four-carbon tert-butyl alcohol.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the ammonolysis of ethyl chloride and the dehydrohalogenation of chlorocyclohexane with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) are the correct reactions.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q36 - Reaction conditions for p-nitro derivative from aniline

questiontext.text: 36. Under which of the following reaction conditions, aniline gives p-nitro derivative as the major product?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Direct nitration of aniline with concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) forms tarry oxidation products and protonates aniline to the meta-directing anilinium ion (\(-\mathrm{NH}_3^+\)), yielding a large proportion of m-nitroaniline alongside p-nitroaniline.

Step 2: Evaluation
To obtain the para-nitro derivative cleanly as the major product, the \(-\mathrm{NH}_2\) group is first protected by acetylation using either acetyl chloride/pyridine or acetic anhydride/pyridine to form acetanilide. The \(-\mathrm{NHCOCH}_3\) group is ortho, para-directing and does not get protonated easily, so subsequent nitration with conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 +\) conc. \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) yields p-nitroacetanilide as the major product (which can then be hydrolyzed to p-nitroaniline). Using dilute \(\mathrm{HCl}\) or direct nitration without protection leads to protonation and substantial meta-nitration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, treating aniline with acetyl chloride/pyridine or acetic anhydride/pyridine followed by nitration with conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 +\) conc. \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) gives the p-nitro derivative as the major product.

answer.text: Acetyl chloride/pyridine followed by reaction with conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 +\) conc. \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\)
Dil. HCl followed by reaction with conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 +\) conc. \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q37 - Reactions belonging to electrophilic aromatic substitution

questiontext.text: 37. Which of the following reactions belong to electrophilic aromatic substitution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) reaction involves the replacement of a hydrogen atom on an aromatic ring by an electrophile.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the bromination of acetanilide, the electrophile \(\mathrm{Br}^+\) substitutes a hydrogen atom on the benzene ring, so it is an electrophilic aromatic substitution. In the coupling reaction of aryldiazonium salts with phenols or aromatic amines, the diazonium cation (\(\mathrm{ArN}_2^+\)) acts as an electrophile and substitutes a ring hydrogen at the para position, which is also an electrophilic aromatic substitution. In contrast, diazotisation of aniline and acylation of aniline take place at the nitrogen atom of the \(-\mathrm{NH}_2\) group rather than on the aromatic ring.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, bromination of acetanilide and the coupling reaction of aryldiazonium salts belong to electrophilic aromatic substitution.
